## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose shifts and OR to implement rotate without loops or conditionals, a common low-level operation.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise shifts and wrap-around semantics
- 32-bit boundary, undefined behavior avoidance
- Performance and portability considerations

## Code Example

```javascript
function rotl32(n, k) {
  return ((n << k) | (n >>> (32 - k))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- What happens if k === 0? How does the expression evaluate?
- How would you implement rotate-right similarly?
- How would you adapt for 64-bit values in a language without native unsigned support?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests non-branching bit-twiddling across a 128-bit value. The triple overlap trick scales beyond 64 bits.

## Key Concepts
- Wide integer bit shifts with zero fill
- Bitwise AND to intersect bit positions
- Non-branching return logic for 0/1 result

## Code Example
```c
unsigned hasThreeConsecutiveOnes128(uint128 x){
  uint128 t = x & (x>>1) & (x>>2);
  return t != 0;
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to decompose a 128-bit value into fixed lanes and reconstruct a rotated layout using only bitwise ops and masking, without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Lane extraction with masks, 32-bit blocks
- Fixed-layout reconstruction; endianness awareness
- Constant-time block-wise permutation

## Code Example
```javascript
uint128 rotateBlocks128(uint128 x) { uint64_t A = x.lo & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t B = (x.lo >> 32) & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t C = x.hi & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint64_t D = (x.hi >> 32) & 0xFFFFFFFFULL; uint128 r; r.lo = (A << 32) | D; r.hi = (C << 32) | B; return r; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to generalize to n blocks or different block sizes?
- How to ensure correctness on little- vs big-endian targets?
- Could you adapt this for a compile-time constant permutation table?
